questions.question: In a circular seating arrangement, why can't positions be described with a fixed "left" or "right" the way a row can?
options: There is no fixed starting point, so positions are described relative to each other (clockwise/anticlockwise, opposite, neighbour)
Circular arrangements are never used in exams
Everyone in a circle always faces the same direction as in a row
Circular arrangements only ever have 4 seats
questions.rationale: Unlike a row, a circle has no natural start or end, so clues use relative terms like clockwise, anticlockwise, immediate neighbour, or opposite rather than absolute left/right positions.

questions.question: Why does it matter whether a circular group is "facing the center" or "facing outward"?
options: It doesn't matter — clockwise is always the same either way
Facing outward means there are no neighbours
Facing outward reverses how clockwise/anticlockwise appears from each person's own point of view
This only matters for row arrangements, not circular ones
questions.rationale: Clockwise motion looks reversed from each person's own perspective depending on whether the group faces the center or faces outward, which changes how directional clues like 'immediate right' should be applied.

questions.question: When solving a seating arrangement, which type of clue should generally be placed first?
options: Vague count-based clues like 'as many people between A and B as between C and D'
Absolute-position clues like 'sits third from the left' or 'sits at an extreme end'
Clues about people not mentioned elsewhere
It never matters what order you use the clues
questions.rationale: Absolute-position clues fix a person's seat directly with no dependency on other placements, so working from them first gives a stable anchor before applying relative or comparison-based clues.

questions.question: In a double-row arrangement where the two rows face each other, how does 'left' and 'right' behave between the rows?
options: It's identical in both rows
Only the front row has a left/right
Left and right don't apply to double rows
It is mirrored — what's to one row's left is to the opposite row's right at the same paired position
questions.rationale: Because the two rows face each other, their left/right orientation is mirrored, so a seat and its opposite-row counterpart have reversed left/right relationships.

questions.question: In a circular seating arrangement facing the center, how does clockwise motion appear compared to a group facing outward?
options: Reversed compared to facing outward
Identical in both cases
Only relevant for double-row arrangements
Clockwise doesn't apply to circles
questions.rationale: Facing the center versus facing outward reverses how clockwise/anticlockwise motion appears from each person's own point of view, which changes how directional clues should be applied.

questions.question: What type of clue is 'X sits exactly between A and B'?
options: A relative clue with no fixed position
An absolute clue fixing X's position relative to two already-placed people
A count-based comparison clue
It cannot be used until the very end
questions.rationale: 'Exactly between' fixes an absolute middle position once A and B's positions are known, making it one of the higher-priority clues to place early, alongside extreme-end and numbered-position clues.

questions.question: In a double-row arrangement where the rows face each other, what does 'sits opposite to' link?
options: Two seats within the same row
A seat in one row to a seat at the same paired position in the other row
Only the two extreme ends
Nothing — 'opposite' isn't used in double rows
questions.rationale: In a double-row arrangement, 'opposite' links a seat in one row directly to the seat at the same paired position in the facing row.

questions.question: According to the step-by-step building process, which clues should generally be placed last?
options: Absolute-position clues like 'third from the left'
Extreme-end clues
Vague count/comparison clues like 'as many between A and B as between C and D'
Immediate-neighbour clues
questions.rationale: Count/comparison clues are best saved for last since they mainly eliminate remaining options rather than fixing a position directly, and work best once most seats are already filled.

questions.question: What does 'Y is a neighbour of X' mean, as opposed to 'Y sits immediately to the right of X'?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
'Neighbour' means adjacent on either side; 'immediately right' specifies one exact direction
'Neighbour' only applies to circular arrangements
'Immediately right' means anywhere in the row
questions.rationale: 'Neighbour' is a non-directional adjacency clue (either side), while 'immediately right of' fixes one specific direction — conflating the two can lead to placing a person in the wrong seat.

questions.question: If a single clue creates two possible valid arrangements, what is the recommended approach?
options: Guess one and move on
Discard the clue as invalid
Keep both arrangements as branches and use the next clue to eliminate one
Restart the whole puzzle from scratch
questions.rationale: When a clue is ambiguous, the reliable approach is to keep multiple candidate arrangements in mind and let a later clue eliminate the incorrect branch, rather than guessing early.
